q: Calculate the signal concentration per million cells at 2 h and at 8 h. Comment on your answer.
0.4 / 4 = 0.1 and 20 / 200 = 0.1 nmol dm⁻³: the same, so each cell releases the same amount and the signal rises in proportion to cell density.
Estimate the signal concentration needed to switch on light.
Between 1.5 and 6 nmol dm⁻³ (light starts between 4 and 6 h).
Explain why the mutant never glows on its own but glows when signal is added.
It still has the receptor and the light genes, but cannot make the signal. Added signal binds the receptors and switches on the light genes.
Suggest the advantage of making light only at high density.
A few cells make too little light to be useful, so making light then would waste ATP; at high density (in a squid’s light organ) the glow is bright enough to work.
Predict the light output if normal bacteria grow in a tank where the medium is constantly replaced. Explain.
Little or no light, even at high density: the signal is washed away and never reaches the threshold.

22.t: Working with data: insulin and muscle cells
q: Calculate the percentage increase in uptake by normal cells from 0 to 200 pmol dm⁻³ insulin.
Explain why uptake by normal cells levels off at high insulin.
All the insulin receptors are occupied, so all available GLUT4 transporters have already moved into the membrane: transport is at its maximum.
Explain why uptake is not zero without insulin.
Some glucose transporters are always in the membrane, whatever the insulin level.
Compare the two curves and suggest one cause of the difference.

Resistant cells take up less glucose at every concentration and need far more insulin for the same uptake (about 300 instead of 100 pmol dm⁻³ for 58 units). Cause: fewer receptors, or a fault in the signalling chain inside the cell, so fewer GLUT4 move to the membrane.
People with insulin resistance often have high insulin in their blood. Use the data to suggest why.
The pancreas releases more insulin to compensate: at 400–800 pmol dm⁻³ resistant cells reach near-normal uptake.
